title: The Measure of the King's Foot (MR)
summary: A fawning courtier suggests that all land in the empire should be measured using Emperor Akbar's royal foot. Birbal shows the comical chaos of such flattery. [MR]
full_text:
A fawning courtier named Mirza Dawood, seeking to flatter Emperor Akbar, proposed a grand imperial reform in the council hall:

'Your Imperial Majesty! Currently, land across our provinces is measured using standard wooden cubits and iron chains. What an insult to your majesty! I propose that henceforth, by imperial decree, the official unit of land measurement throughout Hindustan shall be the exact length of Your Majesty's royal foot!'

Akbar was intrigued: 'A royal foot? It sounds noble. What say you, Birbal?'

Birbal bowed with a serious expression: 'Sire, Mirza Dawood's devotion is magnificent. But before we mandate this law across thirty provinces, we must test how it works in practice.'

Birbal brought a royal tailor and had Emperor Akbar's foot measured with an ivory ruler. The royal foot measured precisely eleven inches.

Birbal then ordered two imperial surveyors to measure a parcel of land in the palace garden using the Emperor's current foot measurement.

Next, Birbal turned to the courtier: 'Mirza Dawood, what happens when winter arrives, and His Majesty wears thick wool socks and heavy riding boots? The royal foot becomes thirteen inches long!'

'And what happens when His Majesty takes off his shoes to bathe in the river? The foot becomes ten inches!'

'And what happens in twenty years, when His Majesty's noble son ascends the throne, whose foot may be nine inches long?'

Birbal turned to Akbar: 'Sire! If we measure land by the Emperor's foot, every field in Hindustan will expand in winter, shrink in summer, and change borders with every new monarch! Boundary walls will have to be torn down every autumn, and every farmer in the empire will be in perpetual lawsuits over shifting inches!'

Akbar stared in realization, then burst into hearty laughter: 'By Allah, Birbal! You have saved my empire from measuring madness!'

Akbar rejected the courtier's foolish flattery, keeping the standard measurement of land fixed and equitable for all.
